name: Woozle effect
statement: Repeated citation turns a weak or absent finding into an accepted fact, because each new citation reads as fresh support rather than a repetition of the same source.
meaning: The claim is about a literature rather than a person. A finding is stated once, tentatively or not at all, and later papers cite it. Later papers cite those. To an author arriving in the field, the pile of references looks like a body of evidence, so the claim is repeated again and the pile grows. Gelles called this evidence by citation. Two things make it hard to see from inside. No single step is dishonest, since every author cites a real document that really says what is attributed to it. And the pile grows faster than the data, because a review paper can be cited for a claim without containing any measurement of it. What ends up carrying the belief is the shape of the citation graph, not the strength of the studies at its root.

origin.where: Journal of Marriage and the Family
origin.note: Gelles reviewed a decade of family violence research and described claims that had gained standing through repeated citation rather than through new data. Nielsen's 2014 paper, which is the source used here, credits the phrase woozle effect to Beverly Houghton, who used it in a paper on research on women and abuse at the American Society of Criminology conference in Philadelphia in November 1979. The woozle is from chapter three of Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh, in which Pooh and Piglet circle a spinney of larch trees tracking paw marks that multiply as they walk. Christopher Robin points out that the tracks are their own.

evidence: The measured case is Steven Greenberg's 2009 citation network. He took the claim that beta amyloid is produced by and injures muscle in sporadic inclusion body myositis, collected every English language PubMed paper carrying a statement about it, and recorded which paper cited which for that statement. The network held 242 papers and 675 citations, of which 636 were supportive, 18 neutral and 21 critical. Counting chains rather than single links, 220,553 citation paths supported the claim against 28 that weakened it. Between 1996 and 2007 supportive citations grew sevenfold and supportive paths 777-fold. Six primary data papers held results that weakened or refuted the claim and were barely cited. Three of them, from independent laboratories, covered 35 patients: 28 had no affected muscle fibres and the other seven had five or fewer, in sections that hold thousands. Seventeen animal and cell culture papers made 32 citations to primary data, 31 of them to the four supportive papers and one to the six critical ones. One review paper carried 63% of all citation paths and four reviews by a single research group carried 95%. Greenberg also traced invention. One subclaim about timing appeared in 27 papers on 37 citations, nine of which pointed at papers saying nothing about timing. Seven papers made 17 citations to 12 conference abstracts dressed as peer reviewed papers. Rebuilding the network with the bias against critical content removed gave authority status to five of the six neglected papers. Vedrana Pavlovic and colleagues measured citation accuracy directly, asking the authors of cited papers to check. Across 2,526 citations to 14 heavily cited papers, and a verification set of 4,912 citations to 13 more, at least one inaccurate citation appeared in 11% and 15% of citing articles. The commonest fault, at 38.4%, was citing a finding the source did not contain. One-fifth of the inaccurate citations came from chains of earlier inaccurate citations. Tzu-Kun Hsiao and Jodi Schneider looked at what happens after a paper is withdrawn: of 13,252 citation contexts written after a retraction, 722, or 5.4%, mentioned the retraction.

replication.headline: Greenberg's network design has since been run on six other biomedical questions, and four of the six showed citation bias.
replication.detail: Miriam Urlings and colleagues built citation networks for six biomedical research questions, mapped every citation that could have been made against those actually made, and modelled what predicted a citation. Four of the six networks showed evidence of citation bias. Self-citation, the authority of the corresponding author and journal impact factor raised the chance of being cited in all six. The surrounding literature is much larger. Bram Duyx and colleagues found 52 studies of citation bias and pooled the 21 that reported enough data. Articles with statistically significant results were cited 1.6 times as often as articles without, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.8. Across eight studies, articles whose authors concluded they had found support for their hypothesis were cited 2.7 times as often, CI 2.0 to 3.7. Heterogeneity was high and its source was not identified, and of the 52 studies 29 found a clear effect of outcome on citation, 11 found none and 12 were mixed. The authors report that almost all pointed the same way. What has not carried over is Greenberg's fuller account. Janina Sarol, Jodi Schneider and Halil Kilicoglu tried to rebuild his coding automatically on the same amyloid network and report that amplification was detectable, while citation bias and invention were not.

study.cite: Urlings, M. J. E., Duyx, B., Swaen, G. M. H., Bouter, L. M., & Zeegers, M. P. (2021). Citation bias and other determinants of citation in biomedical research: findings from six citation networks. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 132, 71-78.

limits: Greenberg studied one claim in one specialty, and one colleague validated his text and citation extraction for 17% of the papers. His analysis shows how the claim acquired authority. It does not test whether the claim is true, and he does not say it is false. The full text of Urlings and colleagues is paywalled, so the four-of-six figure here is read from the abstract at the Vrije Universiteit repository, which does not name the six research questions. Gelles's 1980 review was not obtained either, and the account of his argument and of Houghton's 1979 coinage comes from Nielsen. The most quoted single case is a five sentence 1980 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine reporting that addiction was rare among hospital inpatients given narcotics, counted by Leung and colleagues in 2017. That correspondence is paywalled. Hao, Davis and Schatman give its result as 608 citations through 2017, 439 of them treating the letter as substantive evidence, and that is the route by which those two numbers reach this page. No experiment was located in which readers were shown a claim backed by many citations or by few and their belief measured, which is the form a psychological test of the effect would take. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and Google via web search.
misreadings: The spinach story is the example most often reached for, and the standard telling of it is itself a woozle. Rekdal traced the chain. Arnold Bender said in a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College that the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point, and repeated the phrase in a book and an article three years later. By a 1977 letter to The Spectator it had hardened to 'appears to have been based on'. Terence Hamblin then printed it as fact in the 1981 Christmas issue of the BMJ with no reference at all, and a 1982 textbook for medical students fixed the error to a specific year, 1870. Mike Sutton asked Hamblin where he had read it; Hamblin could not remember and thought it might have been Reader's Digest. Rekdal reports no evidence that any decimal point error occurred, and gives Sutton's alternatives: contamination during analysis, and confusion between fresh and dried spinach. Hamblin acknowledged the mistake publicly before his death in February 2012. Telling the spinach anecdote as a documented case of citation drift commits the error it is offered to illustrate. A second misreading treats Greenberg as having disproved the amyloid claim. He argues the opposite of certainty: with the citation bias removed, belief in the claim's truth and its falseness would be balanced. The figure that only about 20% of citers have read what they cite is also weaker than it sounds. Simkin and Roychowdhury inferred it from the way misprints repeat across reference lists, so it is the output of a stochastic model rather than a count of readers. Pavlovic and colleagues' 11% and 15% are counts. And the Pooh story is about self-deception. The extra tracks belong to Pooh and Piglet, laid down as they circle the spinney, which makes it a picture of self-citation rather than of borrowing from strangers.
